name: Filter design: types, resonance, key-tracking, filter banks and envelopes
goal: Choose and drive filters musically: LP/BP/HP/notch morphing, ladder/diode/comb flavours, resonance, key-tracking, velocity and envelope amount, parallel/serial and multi-band filter banks, talking/formant filtering and sample-rate reduction.

theory: Subtractive synthesis removes harmonics from a rich oscillator; slope (12/24 dB/oct) sets steepness; resonance boosts the cutoff band (self-oscillates at high Q); cutoff = base + env*amount + keytrack*note + LFO.
prerequisites: Ability to duplicate the post-filter (or post-amp) path into discrete L and R chains
Clock-synced LFO, step sequencer for modulation values, slow random source, delay and a crossover/HP split
DAW or synth FX rack supporting parallel chains/buses; dual filters; tempo-syncable LFO or step/rhythm modulator; optional bus compressor

Engine with per-voice oscillators that each have an envelope, and assignable filters (Web Audio: per-oscillator GainNode envelopes and BiquadFilterNodes; fixed vs key-tracked frequency set in code, implementation note)
Filterbank with ≥10 bandpass bands and per-band gain (any multiband/EQ plugin with automation, or Web Audio: 12 BiquadFilterNodes per channel with gain lanes, implementation note)
Hardware knobs or a MIDI controller with MIDI-learn
Hybrid synth or Traveler-inspired Web Audio engine with multi-osc, stereo filter, envelopes, LFOs/mod matrix, sequenced control tracks (or automation), and FX (EQ/chorus/delay/reverb)
Hybrid synth or Web Audio filters exposing multiple models (ladder/diode/comb/formant) or approximations

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: Rendered part or recipe following the workflow

constraints: Portable recipe; not affiliated with any vendor; do not copy factory presets or sample packs.
Numbers in variants come from the source video transcripts; workflow steps are the consolidated mainstream practice.
Bring drums in early and avoid pitch wobble unless asked (user preferences from daily tests).

steps.action: Choose type: LP for warmth, HP to thin, BP for focused/telephone, notch/comb for hollow; ladder = fat/rounded, diode = squelchy.
Set cutoff and resonance (Q 0.7 neutral; 3-8 vocal/acid); enable key-tracking 50-100% so high notes stay bright.
Filter envelope: fast attack, decay 100-400 ms, sustain low for plucks; scale amount by velocity for dynamics.
Movement: LFO or stepped (S&H) modulation on cutoff, or morph LP->BP->HP->notch with an LFO.
Banks: 2-12 parallel band-passes with independent unsynced LFOs or a stereo step sequence for rhythmic pads.
Formant/talking: band-pass resonances at vowel formants, or resonant filter + sample-rate reduction for robotic speech.
Hear the theory: run `/home/box/audio-tools/bin/python sample-lab/theory/subtractive_filter.py` from the repo root and compare the sections; reuse its functions as a starting point for renders.
steps.expect: WAV in sample-lab/theory/out/ demonstrating the principle

verification: Render a short test and A/B against a reference at matched loudness
Run the generator and confirm it writes a WAV without error
Check mono compatibility and that no element masks the kick/bass

variants.name: Organic alien comb texture: sub-audio saw click train → high-resonance filter → very short, high-feedback delay played by hand
variants.goal: Make an organic alien/sci-fi comb texture bed on most subtractive synths: pitch one saw all the way down until individual saw teeth are heard as a click train, run it through one low-pass at 80–100% resonance, then a delay at full mix with very short time and very long feedback (a comb resonator), adding optional comb filter, moderate pitch modulation and reverb — and perform delay time and cutoff manually (MIDI CC) rather than with modulation for an organic result. Distinct from formant/comb pad recipes that use a dedicated comb filter on sustained oscillators.
steps: Init the patch. Use oscillator 1 only (osc balance fully to osc 1) with a saw.
Turn the semitone/coarse knob all the way down until the saw becomes a click train where each tooth spike is audible.
Use filter 1 only; lower the cutoff a notch and raise resonance to about 80–100%.
Turn the delay mix all the way up, choose a very short delay time and very long feedback.
Play with the delay time while sounds are running to sweep the comb pitch.
Optional variations: add the synth's comb filter mode; add pitch modulation at a moderate speed.
Reduce the delay slightly and add a little reverb on top.
Do not modulate the filter: map cutoff (and FX parameters) to a MIDI controller via MIDI-learn and move them by hand while recording, changing timbre continuously.

variants.name: Stereo from mono: opposite filter frequencies plus inverse amplitude LFO
variants.goal: Widen a mono synth path without Haas delay: split into L/R, offset parallel filter cutoffs in opposite directions (plus/minus frequency spread), then apply a unipolar LFO to left amplitude and its inverse (1−x) to right amplitude so levels see-saw in opposite phase — a modular stereo image that differs from Haas, mid/side EQ, and double-tracked asymmetric processing.
steps: Start from a mono voice (tutorial: two simple waves + white noise → mixer → HP/LP → envelope). Confirm it is centered.

Frequency-spread stereo: put a filter (or filter pair) into a plus/minus or dual-cutoff mode and offset the cutoff so left and right emphasize different bands. This alone creates a static spectral stereo image.
Duplicate the signal into explicit left and right amplitude paths after the envelope (or duplicate the mixer into L/R).

Create a unipolar LFO. Multiply the left path by the LFO. Build the right modulator as inverse unipolar: multiply LFO by −1 then add 1 (or use 1−x) so when left is loud, right is quiet and vice versa. Multiply the right path by that inverse.
Alternate simpler wiring: two attenuators on L and R modulated with opposite depths from the same LFO. Compare against the multiply version — both yield opposite-amplitude stereo.
Audition in stereo and mono. Reduce spread or LFO depth if mono pumps or hollows. Combine later with gentle M/S EQ if lows got too wide.

variants.name: Filter design flavors: ladder, diode, comb, formant
variants.goal: Pick filter *design* (not just LP/HP/BP): ladder/analog-style for classic resonant subtractive tone; diode for EMS/303-ish acid character (retune resonance when switching); formant XY vowel morphs; comb (tiny delayed copy + mix) for peaks/nulls, keyed harmonic shaping, phasing/flanging, and self-oscillation/string-like plucks—then A/B drive+resonance.
steps: Start with standard modes: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch, peak. Note 12 vs 24 dB slopes; many multimode filters morph LP↔BP↔HP (or LP/HP via notch) with blend.

A/B design flavors at same cutoff with LFO on cutoff: raise drive then resonance. Ladder/analog tend similar (ladder often more resonant); ‘dirty’ grit scales strongly with drive; digital may sound harsher or sometimes smoother/controlled.
Try diode model (historically EMS workaround vs Moog transistor ladder; famous in TB-303 acid). Expect different resonance scaling—re-adjust resonance when switching from ladder.
Formant filters: use XY-style controls for vowels (A/O/I/E or A/I/U/O sets); peak strength, spread between peaks, and formant transpose (pitch of the formant structure).

Comb: duplicate + tiny delay + remix → peak/null series. Enable key tracking aligned to pitch to shape harmonics; type semitone offsets carefully to avoid inharmonic chaos unless desired. Resonance can go ±; useful for phasing/flanging-like motion and physical-ish string tones.

Self-oscillation: with enough drive+resonance, ladder/analog/dirty/diode (and comb when tuned) can keep sounding after the osc dies if the note is held; digital/formant typically do not. Use for singing filter tones or comb pluck realism.
Phaser-like filters resemble sparse combs; set pole/notch count via blend, reshape with resonance, add cutoff modulation for classic sweep. Pick model by ear for bass/lead/pad roles.

variants.name: noise and audio-rate filter texture lead
variants.goal: Create a radioactive/unstable cinematic texture or lead: dual detuned saws + WT character, aftertouch bringing in a sharp high oscillator, and mod-wheel sending noise (~30% mix) into audio-rate-style filter modulation (plus optional Osc2→cutoff always-on grit).
steps: Layer two fairly separate saw oscillators plus a wavetable osc for character. Slightly detune one osc; further detune can yield ring-mod-like artifacts.
Optionally enable continuous Osc2 → low-pass cutoff (audio-rate-ish FM-of-filter) for granular grit; A/B it to hear the instability.
Mix noise around ~30%. Map mod wheel to send noise into LPF cutoff modulation — annihilating cutoff with noise yields extremely unstable/distorted color.
Use aftertouch (or pressure) to bring in a high-frequency oscillator for resonant overtones that feel like distortion byproducts when played low.
Play as lead, texture, or pre-scare sting; leave headroom — this patch is intentionally unstable.

variants.name: Morph filter: LFO-cycle one filter continuously through LP → BP → HP → notch → LP
variants.goal: Animate pads, leads and repetitive noisy synths with a single continuous morph filter whose shape glides LP → bandpass → highpass → notch → back to LP, driven by a free-running (non-retriggered) LFO at 20–80% depth, optionally followed by a static classic low-pass, with LFO2 on cutoff and a little per-note random on the morph — a dedicated filter-shape morph recipe, distinct from parallel-filter chains, dual-path stereo spread and filter-flavor (ladder/diode/comb) choice.
steps: Select the morph filter mode. Understand the morph control: 0 = low-pass leaning toward the next shape; at 100 it is fully bandpass, then it continues to highpass, then notch, then back toward low-pass.
Set the slope to 24 dB and add a bit of resonance so the shape changes are clearly visible/audible while sweeping morph by hand.
In the mod matrix route LFO1 → filter morph at 100%, then pull the LFO amount back into the 20–80% range. Turn retrigger OFF so the motion continues across notes.
Pick the LFO rate: slow for pad movement, faster or tempo-synced for rhythmic motion. Then adjust the morph default position, cutoff frequency, LFO amount and rate together to find the sweet spot.
Use the second filter slot as a static classic low-pass after the morph filter to keep the tone in check while the morph adds movement.
Optionally add LFO2 → cutoff frequency (subtle), or replace filter 2 with a second morph filter whose morph is driven by LFO2 (try a different waveform).
For percussive/noisy or robotic repetitive sounds, apply the morph filter with a different LFO waveform and rate to smooth the sound.
Add a small amount of per-note Random (MIDI/mod matrix) to the morph amount/position so each note lands on a slightly different filter shape; A/B with the filter bypassed.

variants.name: Build subtractive 'architectures' from operator pairs: six oscillators with their own envelopes, or three oscillator→own-filter blocks (LP / LP+sub / fixed-frequency HP) into a master bandpass, FM pairs into filters, and series HP→LP
variants.goal: Use a 6-operator engine (or any modular graph) as a configurable subtractive synth in two ways. (A) Six parallel carriers into one master filter, each with its own envelope (VCA before the filter). Layers: two HD saws an octave apart with detune and staggered attacks, a square with LFO-driven PWM, a bright saw with a sharp attack for transient bite, a triangle with width and self-feedback toward saw, and noise whose level is moved by an LFO. Then cutoff, envelope amount, resonance, slight LFO, key tracking, exciter, auto-pan and spring reverb. (B) Turn carriers into filters fed by their modulator to get three independent oscillator→filter blocks: MS-20-style LP with velocity on the envelope; LP with the filter's own sine underneath as a sub; HP switched from key-ratio to fixed frequency for strings, with LFO-driven PWM on the source. All three feed a master bandpass with its own envelope. Then feed FM pairs into the filters for glassy tops, and model classic voice layouts (two oscs in series through HP then LP). The delta vs our multi-envelope level-morph pad is per-oscillator filters, fixed vs key-ratio filter frequency, and FM-into-filter.
steps: Architecture A: choose an algorithm where all six operators are carriers (none modulating each other). Osc 1 = saw (HD/brighter version), osc 2 = saw an octave lower with some detune. Give both full sustain; soften the lower one's attack so it enters more slowly, and add release.

Osc 3 = square with an LFO on pulse width (use a spare LFO, set to taste). Osc 4 = bright, higher saw with a sharp attack envelope for bite. Osc 5 = triangle with width adjusted and some self-feedback (pushing it toward saw), used as the lower layer.
Osc 6 = noise with a slow envelope, and an LFO on its level so it comes in and out.
Master filter: lower cutoff, add filter-envelope amount and resonance, a slight LFO on cutoff and key tracking (cutoff opens up the keyboard). Add exciter, auto-pan and an old-school spring reverb.

Architecture B: pick an algorithm with three carrier/modulator pairs. Turn each carrier into a filter (its own oscillator level down) fed by its modulator set to saw. Block 1: MS-20-style low-pass with resonance, cutoff modulated by its envelope with velocity intensity.

Block 2: another LP fed by a saw, this time keeping the filter operator's own sine mixed underneath. Because the filter's oscillator follows the pitch section, it can act like a sub oscillator (drop its pitch); detune the source slightly.
Block 3: high-pass filter (own mix off) fed by a square, with the filter switched from ratio (key-tracked) to fixed frequency and set by ear for strings, and an LFO on the square's PW.
Send all three blocks into the master filter set to band-pass with its own filter envelope.

FM into filter: change an algorithm so a modulator stacks on an operator that feeds a filter (sine modulators), giving FM spectra into the analog-style filter and then the master filter (try HP or BP on top). For classic layouts, run two oscillators in series through HP then LP (MS-20-like), or a single oscillator into one filter (Polysix-like).

variants.name: Parallel filter chains for rhythmic pad motion
variants.goal: Thicken cinematic pads with parallel processing: run dual filters in parallel (e.g. low-pass + band-pass) with independent rhythmic/LFO cutoff motion synced to tempo, stack overlapping bands that a gentle bus compressor tames, and EQ lows after the parallel stack—portable alternative to only insert-filtering a single path.
steps: Start from layered pad material (body + harmonic spice + optional melodic layer). Route the group into a parallel FX rack rather than only serial inserts.
Create a chain with two filters in parallel mode (example: low-pass on filter 1, band-pass on filter 2) so each path emphasizes different bands simultaneously.
Drive both cutoffs from a tempo-synced rhythm/LFO shape (example: 1-bar custom shape, BPM-synced). Let the two filters move separately so motion is stereo/spectral, not a single sweep.

Expect overlapping bands to stack in level; follow with a compressor on the parallel bus to squash volume spikes from constructive overlap. Prefer fixing sources when possible; bus compress is a lazy safety.
EQ after the parallel filters to remove excess low end created by the stack. Optionally add further parallel chains (saturation, etc.) that may overlap bands—keep compressor/EQ as glue.
Optional stereo trick from transcript: when a rhythm modulator supports stereo shapes, set phase/offset between L/R so upward ramps become opposing L/R motions for width.

variants.name: Talking/vocal formant voice from a resonant filter into sample-rate reduction (sweet-spot aliasing formants)
variants.goal: Create a talking, vowel-like voice without a formant filter: send a harmonically rich oscillator through a filter with healthy resonance and then a sample-rate reducer, find the sweet spots where aliasing creates formants, then animate it with a tempo-synced LFO on cutoff whose rate multiplier is stepped by a sequencer plus slow random modulation of the reduction amount, and send only content above ~1.5 kHz to a delay — a formant-voice delta that differs from formant-filter / spectral-vocode skills.
steps: Patch a harmonically rich oscillator into a filter and add a healthy amount of resonance.
Send the filter output into a sample-rate reduction stage (bit-crusher with sample-rate reduction) after the filter.
Slowly sweep the sample-rate reduction amount (and cutoff) to find the sweet spots where formants appear and the sound starts to 'talk'.
In a patch: sequence the rich oscillator, modulate the filter cutoff with a tempo-synced LFO, and use a step sequencer to change the LFO's rate multiplication per step.
Slowly and randomly modulate the sample-rate reduction amount for different timbres; bring the reducer's wet signal up gradually.
Send only the high frequencies (around 1500 Hz and above) through a delay as an extra layer.

variants.name: Animate a static pad with a stepped 12-band stereo filterbank: assign groups of bands to sequencer patterns (offset ups vs a big down note), set a Q slope with wider low bands and narrower high bands, tame resonant peaks with mild drive plus smoothing compression, alternate bands L/R for width, and use per-band versus group random triggering
variants.goal: Turn a sustained pad into rhythmic, moving texture with a sequenced filterbank of 12 bands per side. Use each band's volume as an EQ to keep what works. Assign subsets of bands to a step sequencer pattern (first five bands, then three frequencies with an offset 'up' pattern, then the last bands as one big down note). Increase the Q globally to get pointed peaks but apply a slope so low bands stay wider and high bands narrower. Add a little drive and a negative 'pull' (compression-style) setting to smooth peaks that blow up at high Q. Spread by sending alternate bands to left and right (sending the same band to both stays mono). Use random triggering per band ('S': each band triggers independently) or grouped ('A': grouped bands fire together) for subtle versus extreme motion. Distinct from our filter-spread and phaser skills: discrete stepped bandpass bank.
steps: Insert the 12-band stereo filterbank on a static pad and use the band volumes as an EQ, turning down only the bands that are too much.
Raise the global Q from fully open (no contour) until the bands become pointed, and apply a slope so low bands are wider and high bands narrower.
Add a little drive and set the compression/'pull' control negative so peaks are smoothed without much distortion.
Assign the first five bands to a step pattern; then unassign them and give three frequencies an offset pattern of up notes; finally give the last bands a single big down note.
Alternate bands between left and right (flip-flop) for stereo spread, choosing the assignment that works in the mix.

Enable random triggering: per-band mode makes each band trigger independently (subtle, dense); grouped mode makes grouped bands fire together (sparser, more extreme). Fine-tune band volumes to contour the result.

variants.name: Buchla 291-style morphing bandpass: 6-pole bandpass with two clocked step sequencers (frequency and bandwidth) as filter snapshots, wet/dry crossfader
variants.goal: Build a free West-Coast-style morphing filter: a steep 6-pole bandpass (bandwidth instead of resonance) fed a harmonically rich complex oscillator, with two clocked, randomized 8-step sequencers — one on frequency (v/oct, ±10 V) and one on bandwidth (0–10 V) — so each clock step jumps to a new 'filter snapshot', blended with the dry signal on a crossfader like an aux, plus optional LFO on the main frequency; copy the voice for a triple morphing filter.
steps: Choose a multimode filter, set it to bandpass and the slope to 6 poles (type the value precisely); set bandwidth to 100%.
Feed a complex oscillator; brighten/complexify it and raise the pitch until the bandpass has harmonics to work with. Sweep bandwidth to hear the change.
Add two step sequencers: one to filter frequency (v/oct), output range ±10 V; one to bandwidth, range 0–10 V.
Put a crossfader after the filter: filtered signal on A, dry signal on B, so the filter acts like an aux/wet-dry morph.
Clock both sequencers, randomize all steps, set 8 steps forward, and run: each step recalls a different frequency+bandwidth 'snapshot'.
Adjust main frequency/bandwidth controls live and optionally modulate main frequency with an LFO via CV.
For a triple morphing filter, duplicate the whole voice (filter + two sequencers) and offset settings.

variants.name: dual stereo filter and LF-width imaging
variants.goal: Shape a cinematic tone with stereo ladder/NJM-style filters, left/right cutoff offset or per-key spread, linked high-pass for band-pass effects, and low-frequency width so bass stays centered while highs move.
steps: Choose ladder-style LPF slope from gentle 6 dB to steep 24 dB (four ladder variants) OR NJM 2069-style model for DW/Poly-era character.
Enable stereo filter path. Offset left vs right cutoff, or use automatic per-key spread, for subtle stereo timbre differences (good automation target).
Add dedicated high-pass; optionally link HP to primary cutoff for band-pass style sweeps. Set keyboard tracking and envelope amounts for both LP and HP.
Output section: set pan-spread so successive voices fan across the stereo field; optional random voice position.
Engage low-frequency width / LF-width: narrow pan of content below ~middle C so bass stays mono-centered while upper spectrum keeps stereo motion.
Optional vintage/voice-offset knob for slight per-voice drift of tune, mixer, filter, envelopes — keep near 0 for clean cinematic pads.

variants.name: Three-band parallel bandpass filter-bank pad with offset, unsynced cutoff LFOs
variants.goal: Build a pad from bandpass filters instead of low-pass: saw (+ octave-down second osc) into three parallel resonant bandpass filters set low / mid / high, each mixed to the output, each cutoff moved by a slow LFO deliberately offset in phase/value so the three bands never move in sync, then slow-attack pad envelope, ~7-voice unison, chorus and long reverb — a filter-bank pad distinct from parallel rhythmic filter chains and single-bandpass WT pads.
steps: Route oscillator 1 into filter 1, filter 2 and filter 3 in parallel, each also sent to the output. Change oscillator 1 from sine to saw.
Set all three filters to bandpass with a little resonance: filter 1 low frequencies, filter 2 mids, filter 3 highs.
Give it a pad envelope: slow attack, sustain, long release.
On filter 1 cutoff add a slow LFO (global). Copy it to filters 2 and 3 but change the value/start slightly so they don't start the same or synchronize.
Enable oscillator 2 an octave lower, also into all three filters, with the same pad envelope; nudge its speed slightly so the oscillators don't move too evenly.
Add unison ~7 voices, raise volume/bass as needed; resonance amount and output mix are to taste.
Add chorus for thickness and a long-decay reverb; play chords or a single sustained note.

variants.name: Velocity into filter cutoff / filter-envelope amount
variants.goal: Make pads/synths expressive with velocity→filter: set lowest desired cutoff with filter EG amount at 0, raise EG amount (with sustain) for max brightness on hard hits, then map velocity so soft hits stay darker—know your synth’s polarity (many brighten on hard hits; some Moog-style reduce brightness as velocity sens rises).
steps: Init: single bright oscillator (e.g. saw), 24 dB/oct LP, resonance off, filter EG amount 0, keytrack 0. Sweep cutoff to hear range (can go below fundamental).
Set cutoff to the darkest tone you want when the envelope is not pushing (EG amount still 0).
With sustain-full filter envelope, raise EG amount until held notes reach maximum intended brightness (hard-hit ceiling).

Enable velocity→filter (or velocity→filter EG amount). Learn polarity: typical = harder = brighter; some synths (Subsequent/Sub 37 style) increase velocity sens to make soft playing darker instead—strategy reverses.

Play slow soft velocities while raising velocity amount until darkest desired soft tone; verify fast hits still hit the bright ceiling. Trim EG amount if hard hits are too bright; resonance exaggerates the difference.

variants.name: NOOF cinematic synth pulse (Noise, Osc, Osc, Filter): white noise + mono saw + saw an octave up with 5 slightly detuned unison voices, all into a fully closed ladder low-pass opened per note by a fast envelope on an eighth-note MIDI line; automate cutoff as the single energy control
variants.goal: Make a driving film/game synth pulse in any synth with a four-part formula: a white-noise oscillator (a small burst of energy on top), osc A as a plain saw, osc B as a saw one octave up with about 5 unison voices slightly detuned (higher tone and width), and one ladder low-pass with its cutoff all the way down, opened briefly on every note of an eighth-note MIDI line by envelope 2. Then automate one parameter, cutoff, across the track. Low cutoff gives the plain pulse; opening it reveals osc B's width and detune, then the noise burst on top, so a single lane adds or removes energy. Delta vs arrangement cluster's square-osc motor and the filter cluster's velocity→cutoff skill: a layer order chosen so the cutoff reveals width and then noise, giving one-knob energy control.
steps: Noise: enable a white-noise oscillator at a low level as a small burst of energy on top.
Osc A: default saw, one voice.
Osc B: saw pitched one octave up, slightly detuned against osc A, unison about 5 voices with a little detune spread.

Route all three into one ladder low-pass with cutoff fully down. Route envelope 2 (retriggered on each MIDI note) to cutoff with a fast attack and quick decay, so each eighth note opens the filter briefly and it falls straight back.

Automate cutoff through the cue: low = plain pulse (noise and osc B barely audible); higher = osc B width and detune come through; highest = noise burst power on top. Use this single lane to add or remove energy.
Check that muting noise or osc B matters a lot at high cutoff and little at low cutoff. Add effects on top only after the core works.
